thread:
leo: FYI: after we merged the selector tweak to prefer quantized_small kernels, ingress host-side tokenize+parse p95 jumped ~33% in the canary window. Also seeing a ~3x uptick in write syscalls.

ana: ouch. do we have a quick flame or counters? curious if this is allocator churn in the tokenizer or additional syscall churn from more, smaller frames.

leo: flame excerpt from a 60s sample:
```
CPU 60s
  tokenizer/scan.go:emitTokens       20s  (33%)
  parser/frame_parser.go:parse      11s  (18%)
  grpc/transport.go:writevLoop       6s  (10%)
  kvcache/client.go:lookupBatch     3s   (5%)
  selector/score.go:choose          2s   (3%)
```

kai: selector time is small but did it change variant distribution? quantized_small can reduce kernel time but may change output chunk sizes (we pad prefixes differently).

leo: variant breakdown: before canary quantized_small ~7% -> canary 48%. kvcache.hit_rate dropped ~3.6% in same window. grabbed tcp write size hist: median=130B, p95=410B, small_writes(<300B)=66% (baseline 21%).

mia: that explains syscall pressure. New kernel path pads inputs with 16B alignment which increases token boundaries and causes serializer to emit more tiny frames. Also check HPACK/HTTP2 headers: smaller payloads mean headers dominate, so HTTP/2 overhead per-response went up.

ana: interesting point on headers. any change to SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE or padding config recently?

leo: no frame size change. But we did flip the streamer to flush on every completed token under the assumption quantized kernels would be faster. That flush strategy is now amplifying syscalls.

kai: mitigation options: 1) revert the quantized_small bias in canary 2) temporarily change streamer to coalesce until >=512B or timeout 6ms 3) experiment with toggling TCP_CORK on the socket to let kernel coalesce small writes (Linux-only) 4) look at decreasing header overhead (compress or reuse headers)

infra-bot: deploy-canary leo/revert-quantized-bias -> ingress-canary-7 started at 2991234675 :rocket:

leo: rolled a revert in canary and disabled per-token flush. collecting metrics. also enabling tcp_cork on a few test nodes to see if kernel-level coalescing helps.

mia: add ephemeral metrics: host_frame_ops/s, parse_bytes/request, grpc_small_write_rate/s, http2_header_overhead_pct. we need to capture both user-space parse cost and kernel write pressure.

leo: quick after-revert numbers (10m): tokenize+parse CPU -24%, small writes -59%, kv hit-rate back to baseline. p99 stable. TCP_CORK run shows write syscalls drop ~40% and median write-size up to 480B.

kai: good signal. next steps: land fast patch for streamer coalesce default (configurable, default 512B/6ms), add unit test that simulates fragmented input with forced quantized_small selector to reproduce flush pattern, and add selector scoring term for expected_host_frames (estimated from input-size histogram).

ana: also check allocator patterns in tokenizer: quantized path allocates a small temp buffer per token; combining that with more frames can cause more GC/alloc churn. If so, we should pool buffers in the tokenizer path.

leo: noted. I'll add tokenizer buffer pooling to the backlog. Kai, can you sketch the host-framing cost function? We need it in the selector RFC so we can evaluate tradeoffs (kernel runtime vs host IO).

kai: will prototype: expected_host_frames = ceil((expected_output_bytes + header_bytes)/coalesce_threshold). Score += alpha * expected_host_frames where alpha is tuned to match host CPU cost. Filing INF-6207.

infra-bot: canary completed at 2991234899 ✅ 3/3 healthy.

mia: good triage. please add a short incident note in the selector RFC doc describing the cross-layer regression and the mitigations we used (revert, streamer coalesce, TCP_CORK experiment).

leo: PRs: revert + coalesce tests + metrics coming up. I'll include TCP_CORK as an optional runtime knob behind a feature flag for Linux-only environments.

kai: I'll own INF-6207 and work with runtime to add the cost term. Also will export selector.variant_hist by trace-type so we can spot distribution shifts earlier.

ana: one more: add checklist item to kernel-change process: run a streaming-fragmentation harness (real-world traces) and measure host-side write/syscall costs before/after. Kernel-only microbenchmarks miss this.

leo: agreed. thanks team. learning: fast kernel wins can move cost to host if you don't reason about framing and headers.
